extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical geometry / mathematicians studying Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of geometric propositions from Archimedes' On the Sphere and Cylinder I, giving area/volume equalities and inequalities for circles, cones, cylinders and solids of revolution, with constructions using inscribed/circumscribed polygons, similarity, and limiting (bisecting) arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1 — Perimeter of circumscribed polygon greater than circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon is circumscribed about a circle, the perimeter of the circumscribed polygon is greater than the perimeter of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare each pair of adjacent sides touching the circle: for a vertex A touching P,Q on the circle, PA + AQ > arc PQ; apply similar inequality around polygon and sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2 — Construct lines with prescribed smaller ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes AB (greater) and D, one can find two unequal straight lines EG, GH such that EG:GH < AB:D (i.e., a pair of lines whose ratio is less than the given ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure off BC equal to D on BA, pick any line GH and choose AF as a multiple of AC exceeding D; construct EG proportional to AF:AC to GH so that EG:GH < AB:D by componendo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3 — Inscribe and circumscribe polygons to make side-ratio small
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a circle, one can inscribe a polygon in the circle and describe another about it so that the side of the circumscribed polygon has to the side of the inscribed polygon a ratio less than the given ratio of the two magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Prop. 2 to get two straight lines with required ratio, choose a regular inscribed polygon with sufficiently small central angle (bisect diameters repeatedly), then construct corresponding circumscribed polygon via tangents to obtain desired side ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4 — Analogous result for a sector
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a sector, one can circumscribe a polygon about the sector and inscribe another in it so that the side-ratio of circumscribed to inscribed is less than the ratio of the two magnitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same construction as Proposition 3 applied to the sector by repeatedly bisecting the sector's angle to make small equal arcs; circumscribed polygon uses tangents parallel to inscribed sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 — Polygons about a circle with area ratio bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a circle and two unequal magnitudes B (greater) and C, one can describe a polygon about the circle and inscribe another so that the area of the circumscribed polygon to the area of the inscribed polygon has ratio less than B:C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Prop. 2 to get straight lines D,F with D:F < B:C and a mean proportional so D > radius; construct polygons as in Prop. 3 so side ratios yield duplicate ratio (area ratio) less than D^2:F^2 and hence less than B:C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 6 — Same for sectors and controlling remaining segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two unequal magnitudes and a sector (or circle), it is possible to circumscribe and inscribe similar polygons so that the circumscribed to inscribed ratio is less than the given ratio; moreover, by continuing inscribing regular polygons in remaining segments one can make combined leftover segments less than any given area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply iterative bisection (bisect angles repeatedly) to make polygonal approximations; use Euclid XI.2 type argument to make remaining segments arbitrarily small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7 — Surface of inscribed pyramid equals triangle area
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pyramid with an equilateral base is inscribed in an isosceles (right circular) cone, the lateral surface area of the pyramid (excluding base) equals a triangle whose base equals the perimeter of the pyramid's base and whose height equals the perpendicular from the apex to one side of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All perpendiculars from apex to sides of equilateral base are equal; sum of lateral triangular faces gives triangle with base = perimeter and height = that common perpendicular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8 — Surface of circumscribed pyramid equals triangle area
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pyramid is circumscribed about an isosceles cone, the lateral surface of the pyramid equals a triangle whose base equals the perimeter of the pyramid's base and whose height equals the slant side (generator) of the cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base polygon of pyramid is circumscribed about circular base; lines from apex to contact points are perpendicular to polygon sides and equal (generators), so lateral area equals triangle with perimeter base and height equal to generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9 — Triangle from chord less than cone surface portion
rubrics_metrics.description: In an isosceles cone, take a chord AB in the base and join its extremities to the apex O; then the triangle OAB is less in area than the portion of the surface of the cone intercepted between the lines OA and OB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bisect the arc between A and B; compare triangles and surface patches; consider whether the excess of A OAC + A OBC over A OAB is less than or not less than the sum of the segments, and in latter case bisect arcs repeatedly (using Prop. 6) to make segments arbitrarily small and derive inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10 — Two tangent triangles exceed included cone surface
rubrics_metrics.description: If two tangents in the plane of the circular base meet at D and their points of contact joined with the apex O, then the sum of the two triangles formed by OA, OD and OB, OD is greater than the included portion of the surface of the cone between OA and OB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a parallel tangent at midpoint and compare sums of triangular lateral areas vs. cone patches; consider excess G and compare with segments between circle and tangents; if necessary bisect arcs to make remainders small (Prop. 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 11 — Cylinder cut by plane parallel to axis: surface part greater
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane parallel to the axis of a right cylinder cuts the cylinder, the part of the cylinder's lateral surface cut off by the plane is greater than the area of the parallelogram in which the plane cuts it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof follows methods of Props. 9 and 10 (compare inscribed prisms/polygons and use inclusion arguments); original proof not reproduced here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 12 — Parallelograms from tangents exceed included cylinder surface
rubrics_metrics.description: If tangents are drawn at the extremities of two generators of a right cylinder to the circular bases and pairs of tangents meet, the parallelograms formed by each generator and its tangents together are greater than the included portion of the lateral surface between the two generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof follows analogously from Props. 9 and 10 using polygons and inclusion arguments; details omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: General relation — Inscribed/circumscribed pyramids/prisms vs cone/cylinder surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pyramid is inscribed in an isosceles cone, its lateral surface is less than the cone's lateral surface; if a pyramid is circumscribed about a cone its lateral surface is greater. Similarly, inscribed prism lateral surface is less than cylinder lateral surface, and circumscribed prism lateral surface is greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from preceding propositions comparing polygonal faces to circular sectors and using perpendicular equalities and inclusion arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 13 — Cylinder lateral surface equals circle with radius mean proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: The lateral surface of any right cylinder (excluding bases) is equal to a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between the generator (side) of the cylinder and the diameter of its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let CD = diameter, EF = height; let H be mean proportional between CD and EF; show circle with radius H equals cylinder lateral area by contradiction: assume B < S or B > S, construct polygons about B and A and corresponding prisms and use similarity and comparative inequalities to get contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 14 — Cone lateral surface equals circle with radius mean proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: The lateral surface of any isosceles cone (excluding base) equals a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between the slant side (generator) of the cone and the radius of its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let C = base radius and D = side; take H mean proportional between C,D; argue by contradiction using polygons about B and A and pyramids/prisms to show B = S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 15 — Ratio: cone surface to base equals side to radius
rubrics_metrics.description: The lateral surface of any isosceles cone has the same ratio to its base as the side (generator) of the cone has to the radius of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Prop. 14 and the fact that circles are to one another as the squares of their radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 16 — Surface of frustum equals circle with mean proportional radius
rubrics_metrics.description: If an isosceles cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base, the portion of the cone's lateral surface between the parallel planes equals a circle whose radius is a mean proportional between (1) the portion of the side intercepted by the planes and (2) the sum of the radii of the circles in the parallel planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to comparing cones of which the full cone and truncated cone pieces correspond; use Prop. 14 for the two cones and take difference; algebraic manipulation of mean proportionals yields radius of the frustum's equivalent circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 — Ratios of cones/cylinders with equal heights or bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones having equal height have the same ratio as their bases; those having equal bases have the same ratio as their heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical Euclidean proportionality results cited from Euclid used as prior facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2 — Cylinder cross-section proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: If a cylinder is cut by a plane parallel to the base, then the cylinders are to one another as their axes are to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Euclidean result (Euclid XII.13) used as prior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3 — Cones vs cylinders with same bases and heights
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones which have the same bases as cylinders (and equal height) are in the same ratio as the cylinders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an established proposition (used later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 4 — Bases and heights reciprocal proportionality for equal cones
rubrics_metrics.description: The bases of equal cones are reciprocally proportional to their heights; cones whose bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited from Euclid XII.15; used for equality arguments among cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 5 — Triplicate ratio property for cones/cylinders
rubrics_metrics.description: Cones whose diameters of bases have the same ratio as their axes are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters of the bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited from Euclid XII.12 and used in scaling/volume proportionality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 17 — Equality criterion for cones via surface/base/perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: If two isosceles cones are such that the surface of one equals the base of the other and the perpendicular from the center of the first's base on its side equals the height of the second, then the cones are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Prop.15 relating surface:base to side:radius, chain proportionalities and similar triangles to show bases reciprocally proportional to heights and thus cones equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 18 — Solid rhombus of two cones equals a cone with given base and height
rubrics_metrics.description: Any solid rhombus consisting of two isosceles cones (joined on a common circular base) is equal to the cone whose base equals the surface of one of the component cones and whose height equals the perpendicular from the apex of the other cone to one side of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct auxiliary cones with bases equal to surfaces of components and equal heights; use Lemma 1 proportionalities to equate cones and show equality of volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 19 — Removing rhombus yields cone equal to surface-of-frustum-based cone
rubrics_metrics.description: If an isosceles cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base, and on the circular section a cone is described with apex at the base centre, then removing the formed rhombus from the whole cone yields a remainder equal to the cone with base equal to the surface of the frustum and height equal to the perpendicular from the centre of the base to a side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct cones whose bases equal surfaces of the whole cone and its sections and use equality decompositions (Prop.18) along with equal heights to conclude the required equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 20 — Analogous rhombus difference for rhombus formed with other apex
rubrics_metrics.description: If one cone of a rhombus is cut by a plane and a cone is described on the resulting section with the same apex as the other cone, removing the resulting rhombus from the whole rhombus leaves a solid equal to the cone whose base equals the surface of the portion cut off and whose height equals the perpendicular from the other apex to the side of the first cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar construction and decomposition to Prop.19, swapping which apex is used; invoke Prop.18 and proportionality lemmas to equate volumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 21 — Sums of parallel chords relate to diameter and chord ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: For a regular polygon of even number of sides inscribed in a circle with AA' a diameter and pairs of opposite vertices joined by parallels (BB', CC', ...), (BB' + CC' + ...):AA' = A'B:BA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw parallels and use similar triangles to equate ratios between segment sums intercepted on AA' and chord divisions; sum analogous equal ratios to obtain stated proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 22 — Polygon in a circular segment: parallel sum ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: If a polygon with an even number of equal non-base sides is inscribed in a circular segment and lines parallel to the base join pairs of vertices, then (sum of those parallels):AM = A'B:BA where AM is distance from apex to base midpoint and A' is diameter through midpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Prop.21: construct parallels, join transversals, use similar triangles and summation of ratio equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 23 — Revolution of polygon in great circle produces inscribed solid with smaller surface than hemisphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a regular polygon (number of sides multiple of four) inscribed in a great circle; revolving the polygon and the circle about a diameter AA' causes interior polygon points (excluding A,A') to trace circles on the sphere and sides to trace parts of conical surfaces; the hemisphere's surface is greater than the surface described by the revolution of the inscribed polygon (because the hemisphere entirely includes the revolved polygonal surface with same planar boundary and same concavity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare hemisphere and the revolved inscribed figure: same planar boundary, inclusion and same concavity imply hemisphere surface greater (Assumptions 4). Apply to both halves to conclude sphere surface greater than inscribed revolved figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 24 — Surface of revolved inscribed polygon equals circle with radius from chord-sum rectangle
rubrics_metrics.description: For such a revolved inscribed figure (polygon number of sides multiple of four), its surface equals a circle whose squared radius equals BA*(BB' + CC' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the revolved figure into conical pieces; apply Prop.14 and Prop.16 to express each piece as a circle and sum; since BA = BC = ... obtain total circle radius via sqrt(BA*(sum of parallels)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 25 — Surface of revolved inscribed figure less than four times great circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the figure inscribed in a sphere by revolving a regular polygon (4n sides) is less than four times the greatest circle in the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Prop.21 to relate sum of parallels to diameter and chord lengths; algebraic manipulation gives radius^2 = AA'*A'B < (diameter)*(diameter) so total surface < 4 * great circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 26 — Volume of revolved inscribed figure equals cone with base = its surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid of revolution formed by revolving the inscribed polygonal figure is equal in volume to a cone whose base is a circle equal to the surface of that figure and whose height equals the perpendicular from the sphere centre to one side of the polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the solid into rhombi and cones (Props.18 and 20) with equal heights p; add volumes using cone proportionality to conclude total equals a cone of height p with base equal to sum of surfaces (the surface of the solid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 27 — Inscribed revolved solid volume < 4 times certain cone
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure inscribed as above is less than four times the cone whose base is a great circle and whose height is the sphere radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By Prop.26 volume equals cone with base equal to surface of solid and height p (perpendicular to side); since surface < 4*great circle (Prop.25) and p < sphere radius, volume < 4 * reference cone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 28 — Revolving a circumscribed polygon produces solid greater than sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: If a regular polygon (multiple of four sides) is circumscribed about a great circle and revolved about AA', the resulting circumscribed solid is greater than the sphere itself; each polygonal side's revolved portion contains the corresponding circular segment surface, so the total circumscribed figure exceeds the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare for each circular belt: the revolved polygonal part entirely includes the revolved circular segment with same boundary and concavity, so by Assumption 4 the polygonal surface exceeds the circular segment; sum over all parts to get greater total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 29 — Surface of circumscribed revolved figure equals circle with radius from chord-sum rectangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of the circumscribed revolved figure (as in Prop.28) equals a circle whose squared radius equals AB*(BB' + CC' + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The circumscribed figure is inscribed in a larger sphere; apply same decomposition and Prop.24 argument to that larger sphere to derive formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 30 — Surface of circumscribed revolved figure > four times great circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The surface of a figure circumscribed as above about a sphere is greater than four times the great circle of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relation from Prop.21 and Prop.29 to show resulting radius > diameter of great circle, hence area > 4 * great circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 31 (numbered 91 in text) — Circumscribed solid equals cone with base equal to its surface
rubrics_metrics.description: The solid of revolution circumscribed about a sphere (as in previous propositions) is equal to a cone whose base equals the surface of the circumscribed solid and whose height equals the sphere radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Prop.26 for the circumscribed case: the revolved circumscribed solid is inscribed in a larger sphere and can be decomposed into rhombi/cones whose volumes sum to a cone of height equal to sphere radius and base equal to the solid's surface; corollary gives it's > 4 times the comparison cone.
